newsitem.title: USA: Clinton claims credit for Louisiana crime drop.
newsitem.headline: Clinton claims credit for Louisiana crime drop.

text.p: President Bill Clinton stumped in his native South on Thursday, claiming credit for fighting crime and shrugging off new character attacks from Republican Bob Dole.

At a rally at the Marrero Action Playground in Jefferson Parish, Clinton told Louisiana supporters his programme aimed at hiring 100,000 police officers had helped lead to a dramatic reduction in violent crimes and drug crimes in what has been a high-crime neighbourhood.

"This is an example of what we can do when we stop talking and start acting," he told an enthusiastic crowd, asserting that he had taken "crime fighting out of politics" while attacking Republicans for wanting to change his programme.
Under constant attack by Dole for rising drug abuse among teenagers, Clinton fired back that Republicans tried to cut back on a programme aimed at creating safe and drug-free schools.

"Drug use is going down in America, folks, big time, but drug use among children under 18 is still going up. The last thing we need to do is cut back on the safe and drug-free schools effort," he said.
He also promoted his proposal for making teenagers take a drug test as part of obtaining a driver's license.
On a warm Indian summer day, Clinton took his confident re-election campaign through a region that has been staunch Republican territory in recent years.

He visited Alabama for the first time as president as part of a two-day swing that also took him to Louisiana, and on Friday, will go to Georgia. Alabama has not gone to a Democratic presidential candidate since Jimmy Carter won it in 1976. Dole has a narrow lead in the state.
Clinton, appearing on the campus of Birmingham-Southern College, said the thousands in the crowd indicated to him that Alabama wanted to help him "build a bridge to the future."
"It is such a beautiful day and the crowd is so large, maybe Alabama is going to come along with me on that bridge," he said.
Clinton later flew to Louisiana, where he holds a sizable lead.
Speaking to a crowd outside the training hangar of Northrup Grumman Corp., in Lake Charles, he made only an oblique reference to a savage attack from Dole on Thursday in Florida.
"I'm glad I've run a campaign of ideas, not insults, to give you the ideas of what I'll do in the next four years if my contract is renewed in less than two weeks from today," Clinton said.

The Clinton campaign said it was mystified by Dole's failed appeal to third-party candidate Ross Perot to drop out of the race. "There's no reason to believe that that would be a useful initiative," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry.

A native son of the South, born and raised in Arkansas, Clinton would seem to hold a natural advantage in the region but that has not been the case. The South has grown more conservative over the years and did not rally behind Clinton in his 1992 campaign.

But the Clinton campaign team does not want to cede any territory to the Republican challenger even though Clinton has landslide-type leads elsewhere in the race for 270 electoral votes and victory on Nov. 5. Dole was also in Alabama and Louisiana on Thursday.

In Birmingham, a knot of Dole supporters greeted Clinton on his motorcade route to Birmingham-Southern. "Dole bled, Clinton fled," said a sign held up by one, referring to Dole's Second World War history and Clinton's avoiding of the Vietnam War draft.

In his speech, Clinton adopted an aw-shucks, down-home manner, saying he did not like to attack Dole because "the way I was raised my momma woulda whipped me if I ever said I was better than somebody else."
"This is not a question of who's bad, it's a question of what's right for our future," he said.
